sub_themes.sub_theme: ML weather models on unprecedented extremes

insights.claim: Data-driven weather models capture record heatwave patterns but underestimate peaks, with error growing beyond the prior record.
Peak underestimation persisting at one-to-two-day leads points to a magnitude ceiling rather than simple error growth.
ML failures on rare storm tracks conflate training-data rarity with loss-induced smoothing, which matched comparisons could disentangle.
Strong average skill scores do not make ML weather models ready for warnings on the highest-impact events.
A fixed set of out-of-sample record events would let model developers test extreme-magnitude skill themselves.
Post-processing calibration is a cheaper first remedy than probabilistic retraining for under-dispersed ML weather ensembles.
Per-gridpoint ensemble calibration destroys spatial coherence, undermining regional metrics such as heatwave area.
Member-by-member rescaling with lead-time-dependent inflation can fix spread while keeping spatial fields coherent.
Calibration that works on average remains overconfident at high thresholds, entangling calibration with the extremes problem.
If ML ensembles are most overconfident when most biased on record events, post-processing alone cannot fix them.

sub_themes.sub_theme: GPU job packing for small experiments

insights.claim: Bin-packing small training jobs onto shared GPUs by profiled memory and compute footprint sharply raises cluster utilisation.
Profiling must include evaluation steps, with per-process caps and history-based margins, to protect co-located jobs.
Internal research tools spread best as two-way exchanges where adopting labs contribute adapters back.

adjacent_ideas.claim: An extremes benchmark could score tail reliability of calibrated ensembles, not just deterministic peak error, on record events.
Ensemble inflation conditioned on forecast distance beyond the prior record might partially offset the extrapolation ceiling.
Packed small-GPU sweeps could make systematic loss-function ablations on extreme-magnitude bias affordable without full retraining budgets.
